title: AVALANCHES
subtitle: There are more than a million avalanches worldwide every year. They are dangerous and unpredictable. Once triggered, they can travel at speeds of up to 400 kilometres per hour. Experts using the latest technology, research and training are working to forecast them with greater accuracy

paras: Snow is complex. From the moment it leaves the sky, its form constantly changes. The factors determining if it falls as powder or wet slush, and whether it is likely to cause hazardous conditions and a possible avalanche, are subtle. Some of the most advanced avalanche research in Europe is being performed by teams in Grenoble, the so-called capital of the Alps. One such team comes from the CEN, the French Centre of Snow Studies. CEN is part of Météo-France, the French weather station, and compiles a daily ‘Bulletin of Avalanche Risk’, the BRA, throughout the ski season.

Out on the mountains around Grenoble are 140 observation posts, mostly between 1,500 metres and 2,000 metres above sea level. Readings are taken twice a day by teams of snow experts known as ‘nivologists’. They record the conditions of clouds, wind, temperature, precipitation, thickness and quality of fresh snow, total height of snow on the ground, and whether any avalanches have been observed since the last readings. At least once a week, surveys are carried out to evaluate the stability of the snow cover on the ground. Samples are ‘cored’ out using a cylindrical tool, and the various layers of snow studied minutely by analysing the way they are bonded, and the shape of their crystals.

Together, the twice-daily observations and the weekly surveys overlap into what is known as the ‘nivo-weather network’ and are used to create the BRA, which is distributed to ski resorts throughout France. Other European countries and parts of America and Canada have their own equivalents of the BRA, and there is a standard scale for recording levels of risk to avoid miscommunication.

What causes an avalanche? Several factors determine when, and whether, a mass of snow will stay bound to a slope or slide downhill as an avalanche. One of these is the slope gradient. About 90 per cent of all avalanches start on slopes between 35 and 40 degrees. Slopes above the treeline facing away from the prevailing wind are the most prone to avalanches, as they collect extra snow blown off the windward slopes as well as their own share of snowfall. Trees would help to bind the snow, and anchor it to deep slopes, so preventing avalanches from starting.

Another factor is the trigger, the action that causes the avalanche to start in the first place. Most of the time, this trigger is ‘accidental’. A snowmobile or a skier, maybe a mountain animal such as an elk, will dislodge the fragile layers of snow. But occasionally an avalanche will be triggered ‘spontaneously’, when the burden of snow becomes too much for the slope and it begins to slide with no outside assistance.

Perhaps the most important factor is the way snow crystals form and fall. Ice particles in the air fall as snow and hit the ground, producing a dense surface layer. This mostly consists of air. Light powdery snow is just 30 per cent water (or ice) and 70 per cent air. Even very wet snow, where water can be squeezed out by the handful, is only between 50 and 60 per cent water. Each snowfall creates distinct layers, as the grains of snow alter depending on weather conditions. For example, warm sunny days cause the snow surface to melt, producing a dense, well-bonded layer over the colder, less dense and relatively poorly-bonded layer underneath. The layers make up what is known as the ‘snowpack’.

The shapes of the snow crystals, their proportions of water to air, and the volume of the snow falling all affect the strength of the bonds holding the snowpack together, which in turn affects the likelihood of an avalanche. A so-called ‘weak layer’ in a snowpack is usually the direct cause of the avalanche, as once this layer releases its tenuous hold on the layer beneath, the snowpack above it breaks away and slides down the mountainside.

Measurements taken from the nivo-network give an indication of avalanche probability in an area, rather than a specific forecast for a particular slope. In Grenoble, the French National Weather Centre has laboratories where models are used to show the way snow falls down different types of slope, using billowing clouds of coloured powder, or displaced snow in a blower. But this type of model, though dramatic to look at, is now being succeeded by computer modelling and mathematical calculations. Météo-France has a study centre in Grenoble with a three-stage chain of computer programs called SAFFRON/CROCUS/MEPRA that creates a series of digital simulations of snow cover and electronically estimates avalanche risk.

With an ever-increasing number of people living and working in the mountains there is a more urgent need for accurate, detailed risk mapping, and reliable avalanche prediction. Then people can learn to manage the avalanches at a local level, building fences and barriers in the correct places, and evacuating homes when necessary with plenty of advance warning.
